Multiple federal courts immediately blocked the order, with one judge calling it 'blatantly unconstitutional.' The administration appealed to the Supreme Court, which refused to fully stay the lower court injunctions while the litigation proceeded. Constitutional scholars from across the political spectrum — including prominent conservatives — agreed the order directly contradicted the plain text of the 14th Amendment as consistently interpreted for 150 years. The order was widely viewed as a deliberate provocation designed to force a Supreme Court reconsideration of birthright citizenship.

original_title: EO 14173 Revokes 60-Year-Old Affirmative Action Contracting Rule

existing.title: EO 14173 Revokes 60-Year-Old Affirmative Action Contracting Rule
existing.description_short: EO 14173 Revokes 60-Year-Old Affirmative Action Contracting Rule
existing.description_long: On January 21, 2025 — his second day in office — Trump signed Executive Order 14173, 'Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity,' which revoked Executive Order 11246, the 60-year-old rule signed by President Lyndon Johnson in 1965 requiring federal contractors to take affirmative action in hiring. The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs was immediately ordered to 'cease and desist all investigative and enforcement activity' and to stop holding contractors responsible for workforce diversity. All pending compliance reviews — including hundreds of federal contractors — were administratively closed. Federal contractors were required to certify in every new contract that they 'do not operate any programs promoting DEI,' with false certifications subject to federal fraud liability. The Congressional Research Service noted the revocation altered legal protections for employees at every company holding a federal contract, covering tens of millions of American workers.

original_title: DOJ Fires Career Prosecutors Who Worked on Trump Investigations

existing.title: DOJ Fires Career Prosecutors Who Worked on Trump Investigations
existing.description_short: DOJ Fires Career Prosecutors Who Worked on Trump Investigations
existing.description_long: On January 27, 2025, Acting Attorney General James McHenry fired more than a dozen career Justice Department prosecutors who had worked on Special Counsel Jack Smith's two federal criminal investigations of Donald Trump. McHenry stated they could not be trusted to faithfully implement the President's agenda because of their role in prosecuting Trump — a rationale that explicitly made professional loyalty to the president, rather than the law, the criterion for employment. Career DOJ veterans described the firings as an egregious violation of norms designed to insulate law enforcement from political manipulation and preserve the independence of federal prosecution. The firings came alongside the reassignment of the department's most senior career official and followed Trump's first-day pardon of January 6 defendants. Legal scholars warned the combination effectively dismantled the DOJ's historic independence and transformed it into an instrument of personal presidential power.
